content_metadata.description: A presentation by Amy Whitaker at Kickstarter HQ exploring the intersection of creativity and commerce.

qAndA.answer: The use of bright colors, dynamic video footage, and thought-provoking images helps to create a sense of excitement and engagement. The personal videos of Amy Whitaker's past work add a touch of vulnerability and authenticity, while the historical footage of Roger Bannister's record-breaking run underscores the power of human achievement. The combination of these elements contributes to the overall content and slightly positive mood of the presentation.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Limitations of business models in creativity.

narrativeProgression.description: Amy Whitaker explains that 'Inventing Point B' involves asking the right questions and challenging assumptions.
She transitions to discussing the challenges of applying business principles to early-stage creative work.
Amy Whitaker emphasizes that the equation of 'price = value' does not apply in the early stages of creative work.

scenes.title: Challenges of Business in Creativity

scenes.contextualRelevance: Potential and challenges of broad access to creativity.

narrativeProgression.description: Amy Whitaker argues that business models often fail to account for the unique qualities of individual artists and the potential for widespread creative talent.
She observes that we live in an age of democratized creativity, but ownership remains concentrated.

scenes.title: Democratization of Creativity

videoEditingDetails.description: The scene transitions back to a shot of Amy Whitaker speaking to the audience
The scene transitions to a blue screen with white text that reads 'We live in an age of the democratization of creativity but not yet in the age of the democratization of ownership.'

scenes.contextualRelevance: Creative approach to business and the role of art in society.

narrativeProgression.description: Amy Whitaker highlights the potential of technology and blockchain to transform work and business models.
She suggests that business models themselves are a design medium, calling for greater understanding and thoughtful design of these models.
Amy Whitaker posits that art serves as a container for independent thinking, emphasizing its political and social significance.
She argues that independent thinking is crucial for a functioning democracy, especially in the current political climate.
Amy Whitaker transitions to sharing a story about Roger Bannister, the first person to run a mile in under four minutes.

scenes.thematicElements: Business Models as Design, Art and Independent Thinking
scenes.title: Business Models and Art

videoEditingDetails.description: The scene transitions back to a shot of Amy Whitaker speaking to the audience
The scene transitions to a white screen with blue text that reads 'Business models are the design medium of our time.'
The scene transitions to a blue screen with white text that reads 'Art is a the container for independent thinking.'

scenes.contextualRelevance: The role of failure and teamwork in creativity.

narrativeProgression.description: Amy Whitaker explains how Bannister achieved his goal by collaborating with his friends, approaching the challenge strategically, and embracing the possibility of failure.
She shows video footage of Bannister's historic achievement.
Amy Whitaker shares a quote from Bannister about the importance of embracing failure in the pursuit of ambitious goals.
She concludes by highlighting how Bannister's story illustrates the power of collaboration, strategic thinking, and embracing the unknown.

scenes.title: Roger Bannister and Creative Process

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm here to talk about something that I think we all experience in a space we all live in,
which is the gray area between creativity and commerce.
It's the topic of a book I wrote that came out in July and the teaching I do at NYU.
So on the one hand, you have art and on the other hand, business.
And when you think about art, there's a kind of stereotype of it, which is a little bit
like watching Marina Abramavik when she was on the stage at the TED conference in 2015.
She represents this stereotypical idea of the artist as other, as a brilliant outsider
who comes in and asks you to put on a blindfold and look meaningfully into the eyes of the
person sitting next to you.
There's also a stereotypical idea of business, men and suits or guys and hoodies, Silicon
Valley, this kind of world of money and power and economics and the mortgage crisis.
Thank you.
Congratulations on your all-male panel.
And there's also in the midst of that, this fantasy overlap of how the two worlds connect.
That is embodied in Daniel Pink's 2004 idea that the MFA was a new MBA.
So this is actually a little bit personal to me because in 2004, I was finishing an MFA
after already having an MBA.
And I was very deeply aware that I could change identity by changing clothes.
So you can say that there is a little bit of narrative coherence involved that stuck
around for about 10 years.
And I resolved it in the short term because I started teaching business to my classmates.
There's never any extra wall space, so I taped the financial times to my paintings.
But there's something else that is going on because I felt pretty weird for a long time
that I had an MFA and an MBA.
But what I think is actually weird is that we don't have a better language to describe
the space in the middle that we all inhabit and how to articulate the space of living
and a vast market economy from the point of view of creativity is the essence of our humanity,
the kind of opposable thumbs of being a person.
So the first thing you need is a little bit more of a Swiss army knife definition of art.
Something that's not about paintings or even Kickstarter projects, but about showing
up to a kind of unknown space in any area of your life, navigating without a template.
And for me, that's defined as a process, not of going from point A to point B, but inventing
point B in any area of life.
And that involves leading from questions as opposed to solutions and taking the risk
of asking the questions that actually matter.
So not, can I design a better airplane, but is flight even possible?
In any area of life, large or small, grand or not grand.
So I think there are a couple of things that come up here on the MBA side that are really
difficult.
Yancey mentioned them earlier, which is that the market is based on an equation of price
equaling value, and it never equals value when you're doing early stage work.
You have no idea if it'll succeed or fail.
You have no idea if you'll do it efficiently.
And business is also standardizing.
Business expects you to be like a big box store.
It doesn't account for your inner artist, or what I believe is the idea that if there's
a modern Leonardo, that exists across all of us.
So there are three observations I want to make about business and art and politics.
And the first is that we live in an age of the democratization of creativity, but not
yet of ownership.
Technology and the blockchain are uniquely poised to change the way that we design our
working lives and to pixelate business models, which means that business models are the
design medium of our time, that we all have a responsibility to understand business well
enough to design the containers around the creative work that we do.
And lastly, I think that art is actually the political medium of our time.
The independent thinking is the greatest lever of power in any democracy, and that that
is the essence of thinking artistically, especially at a time of small talk and the Trump era.
So let me tell one story about art thinking, which is about a man named Roger Bannister,
who's number 41 in the middle, and a project of inventing point B. In May of 1954, Bannister
is the first person ever to run a mile and under four minutes.
So a few things.
He didn't do it by himself.
He did it with his friends who were excellent runners in their own right.
One of them was a world record holder, and he wasn't a professional athlete.
He was training to be a neurologist, and he did these workouts on his lunch break.
He also started the process from a point of failure and gave himself two years to do it,
and he upset a world record that it stood for nine years and only held the record for 45
days, because it's so much easier to see someone do something in best and effort than to
do it yourself.
So my answer to the middle space between creativity and commerce is that it's full of
humanity and going all in before you actually know that something is possible.
And so I hold that forward in the midst of the Big Box Monoculture or the political age,
and I hope that you'll come talk to me after about the language of how you talk about creativity
in the workplace or in your life and how you talk about business, especially in your creative
life, and any inventing point B projects that you're working on.
